d: Aenon; Eusebius and Jerome place this site 8 (Roman) miles south of Scythopolis near the Jordan.

e.t: Aenon is a proper name for a place. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but identifies a specific location mentioned in the Greek New Testament. The name occurs once, in John 3:23, and is rendered “Aenon.” Without the surrounding verse text, its broader significance cannot be stated from the name alone; its basic meaning is the place-name itself.

d: (literal: top of a heap), firstfruits, spoil, treasure (taken in war).

e.t: This word refers to plunder—valuable goods taken as spoils, especially goods gained after victory or conflict. It names what has been seized rather than the act of seizing it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Hebrews 7:4. Its central sense is straightforward: fine spoils or plunder, something of recognized value taken from an opponent or defeated people.

d: Endurable, tolerable.

e.t: This word means “bearable”—something that can be endured or tolerated. It describes a condition or experience as less overwhelming or more capable of being borne. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, all in Matthew and Luke. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains that a situation is bearable rather than unbearable.

me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Masculine, Location Gentilic

e.t: This word identifies someone as Antiochian, meaning “from Antioch.” It functions as a place-based designation, telling the reader that the person is associated with the city of Antioch rather than naming a general character trait or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 6:5. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise role there depends on that context.

d: To carry, bear away (sometimes with violence).
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This word means “to carry away” or “to carry off.” It describes taking something or someone from one place to another, often with the emphasis on removal. In the New Testament, it can describe people being taken away, objects being carried, or someone being brought to another location. The word appears six times in the Greek New Testament, in six verses. Its exact force in any passage depends on what is being carried away and the surrounding sentence.

d: Ram, son of Hezron and father of Amminadab.

e.t: Aram is a personal name, also rendered “Ram.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in Matthew chapter 1. The English forms “Aram” and “Ram” represent the same named individual in these passages. Its precise significance in either verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions simply as a person’s name.

d: Joyfully, with delight, gladly.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word describes doing something with gladness and a warm, willing spirit. It can be rendered “gladly” or “warmly,” expressing positive readiness rather than reluctance or mere outward compliance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 21:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense points to a welcome, cheerful response. It describes how an action is carried out, emphasizing the spirit in which it is done.

d: Suddenly.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “suddenly”: it describes something happening quickly and unexpectedly, without advance warning. It functions as an adverb, telling a reader how or when an event takes place rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Acts. Its precise force in any one verse comes from the surrounding event, but its ordinary sense remains the same: an occurrence that happens abruptly and unexpectedly.

d: A mist, dimness, darkening.

e.t: This word means “mist” or “mistiness”—a thin, cloudlike moisture that makes the air or surroundings hazy. It is a noun describing a visible atmospheric condition rather than an action or quality of a person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 13:11, and its English rendering there is “mist.” The surrounding verse provides the particular significance of the image, but the word itself carries the ordinary sense of obscuring or hazy vapor.

d: Bar-Jonas, son of Jonas, the surname of Simon Peter.

e.t: This word identifies someone as the “son of Jonah,” also rendered “son of Jonas.” It functions as a personal designation rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 16:17, so its meaning is narrowly focused: it names a person through his family connection to Jonah. The wording identifies lineage, while the surrounding verse determines why that designation is used there.

d: To moisten, rain, send rain.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular
Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to rain down,” describing rain falling from above. It functions as a verb, expressing the action of rain being sent or falling rather than naming the rain itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times across six verses, including passages in Matthew, Luke, James, and Revelation. Its basic meaning remains focused on the act of raining, while the surrounding sentence determines who or what is associated with that rainfall.

d: Galatia, a large Roman province in central Asia Minor, comprising the districts of Paphlagonia, Pontus Galaticus, Galatia (in the narrower sense, which some still think is intended in the NT), Phrygia Galatica, Lycaonia Galatica, Pisidia and Isaurica.

e.t: This word is the proper name Galatia, a place mentioned in the New Testament. It identifies the location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The name occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, and each occurrence is rendered “Galatia.” It appears in references from 1 Corinthians, Galatians, 2 Timothy, and 1 Peter, showing that the name is used across several New Testament letters. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: (a) in a clause expressing demand: so, then, (b) indeed, (c) truly.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “indeed” or “so.” It is a small particle used to affirm, emphasize, or draw attention to what is being said. Depending on the sentence, it can add the sense of “indeed” or signal “so” as a connecting emphasis. It occurs five times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in Matthew, Luke, Acts, and 1 Corinthians. Its exact force in any passage is determined by the surrounding words, but its basic function is to strengthen or focus an assertion rather than name an object or action.

d: The base, ground, bottom.

e.t: This word means “ground”—the surface of the earth or the solid land beneath someone. It is a noun naming a physical place rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 22:7. Its basic meaning remains simple and concrete; the surrounding verse determines how the ground functions in that particular sentence. The word is rendered “ground” in the available English translations, agreeing with its direct lexical sense.

d: To lift up, remove, eject.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, iMperative, second, Plural

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to expel,” describing the act of removing someone from a place or group. It expresses a direct action in which a person is sent out rather than allowed to remain. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 5:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical sense is the action of expelling.

d: To put a burden on, to be burdensome.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Subjunctive, first, Singular

e.t: To burden means to place a weight, cost, or demanding responsibility on someone, whether physically or in the wider sense of making life harder. This Greek New Testament word functions as an action word: it describes burdening another person rather than merely naming a burden. It occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, including passages where the idea is translated as burden. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

d: To force forward, run (a ship) aground.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to run aground”—for a vessel to reach shallow ground or shore and become stuck. It describes a specific movement and result rather than a general word for traveling or arriving. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 27:41, and its ordinary meaning is limited to a ship or boat grounding. The surrounding verse supplies the particular circumstances, but the word itself focuses on the vessel becoming grounded.

d: Good-doing, doing of good.

e.t: This word means “doing good”: actively carrying out actions that benefit others or fulfill what is right. It describes good deeds as something practiced, not merely admired or intended. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Hebrews 13:16, so its broader use cannot be established from repeated occurrences. Its central sense remains clear: doing what is beneficial and right as a practical expression of goodness.

d: (Hebrew), Cain, son of Adam and Eve and brother of Abel.

e.t: Cain is the personal name of the man identified in Genesis as Adam and Eve’s son. In the Greek New Testament, this name refers to Cain without being translated into a descriptive title or ordinary vocabulary word. It appears three times, in Hebrews, 1 John, and Jude. Understanding the name itself identifies the person; the surrounding passage determines what aspect of Cain’s story or example is being emphasized in each reference.

d: (a) to come down, either from high land to lower (or actually to the sea-coast), or from the high seas to the coast; hence to arrive at, reach (my destination), (b) of property: to come down (descend) by inheritance to an heir.

e.t: This word means “to come to,” describing movement toward and arrival at a place or destination. It is used in the Greek New Testament for people coming to particular locations, and it can also describe reaching a stated goal. The word occurs 13 times in 13 New Testament verses, most often in Acts, with additional occurrences in 1 Corinthians, Ephesians, and Philippians. Its exact force in any verse depends on the people, place, or goal named in the surrounding passage.

d: Cyrene, a district west of Egypt on the Mediterranean coast, forming with Crete a Roman province.

e.t: Cyrene is the name of a place. As a proper name, it identifies Cyrene rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Acts 2:10, and its meaning remains the geographical name itself. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain how the person or people associated with Cyrene function in that passage; the word alone simply points to Cyrene. d: Reviling, abuse.

e.t: This word means insult or reviling—speech or treatment that abuses, demeans, or attacks another person. It describes hostile verbal behavior rather than a simple disagreement or correction. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times: once in 1 Timothy 5:14 and twice in 1 Peter 3:9. Its use points to conduct that Christians are warned not to return with another insult, but to answer with blessing. The surrounding passage determines the precise situation, while the word itself centers on abusive or contemptuous treatment.

d: Martha, sister of Mary and Lazarus of Bethany.

e.t: Martha is a personal name, referring to a woman named Martha rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 13 times across 12 verses, all referring to this name. It is found in Luke and John, including passages that identify Martha among people known in the Gospel accounts. The name itself does not provide a broader meaning beyond identifying the person who bears it.

d: (properly: to call (summon) to witness, and then absolutely) to testify, protest, asseverate; to conjure, solemnly charge.

e.t: This word means “to testify”: to speak or affirm something as a witness. It describes giving a clear statement that supports what one knows or has received, rather than merely mentioning a subject. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including uses rendered “testify” and “testifying.” Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is bearing witness through spoken affirmation.

d: Sharing, partnership, fellowship.

e.t: This word means “participation” or “something in common.” It describes sharing in something with others—the idea of having a common part, connection, or involvement. As a noun, it names that shared participation rather than an action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 6:14. The surrounding verse context is needed to understand precisely what shared participation is being discussed there.

d: To torment, pain; mid. and pass: to be tormented, pained; to suffer acute pain, physical or mental.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “be anguished” or “to grieve,” describing deep emotional distress and sorrow. It refers to painful grief rather than a mild feeling of disappointment. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, appearing three times in Luke and once in Acts. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is earnest inner distress caused by loss, separation, or troubling circumstances.

d: Anger, wrath, passion; punishment, vengeance.

e.t: This word means “wrath,” referring to anger expressed as a force or condition. It is a noun naming wrath rather than an action someone performs, so it can describe wrath as something people face, experience, or act under in a sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 36 times in 34 verses, from Matthew through Revelation. Its repeated rendering as “wrath” confirms this central meaning, while the surrounding verse determines whose wrath is meant and how it is being discussed.

d: To relax, enfeeble, weaken.

e.t: This word means “to be paralyzed” or “to paralyze.” It describes a condition in which someone is unable to move normally, or the act of causing that condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including descriptions of people who were paralyzed and one exhortation concerning weakened limbs. Its central idea remains physical inability or loss of strength that prevents normal movement. The surrounding verse determines whether it refers to the person affected or the one causing paralysis.

d: To be present, to sit constantly beside, to be near; to have come, arrived.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word describes being present or, in another stated sense, leaving something undone. Its central idea concerns whether someone or something is present, while its wording can also express an action that is not carried out. It occurs 25 times in the Greek New Testament, so it is used across a range of passages rather than being limited to one setting. The surrounding sentence determines which of these related senses is intended in a particular verse.

d: A purple garment, indicating power or wealth.

e.t: This word means “purple,” referring to a rich purple color. It is an adjective-like color term used to describe something that is purple, such as clothing or valuable cloth. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times: twice in Mark, once in Luke, and once in Revelation. Its meaning remains straightforward wherever it appears; the surrounding verse determines what object or garment has this color. The word itself does not carry a broader meaning beyond identifying the color purple.

d: To establish or ratify before.
me: Verb, peRfect, Passive, Participle, Accusative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to establish” or “to establish previously.” It refers to something being confirmed or put in place, with attention to the fact that this establishment has already occurred. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Galatians 3:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is prior establishment or confirmation.

d: A divining spirit, Python, called after the Pythian serpent said to have guarded the oracle at Delphi and been slain by Apollo.

e.t: This word refers to a “divining spirit” or “spirit of divination,” a spirit associated with divination. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Acts 16:16, and functions as a noun naming that kind of spirit. The word itself identifies the spirit; it does not by itself explain the surrounding event, the person’s motives, or the spiritual lesson of the passage. Those details belong to the verse’s context rather than the word’s basic lexical meaning.

d: A fire, pile of burning fuel.

e.t: This word means “fire,” referring to a burning flame or blaze. It is a noun used for the visible phenomenon itself rather than for an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it appears two times, both in Acts 28. The repeated rendering “fire” confirms this straightforward sense. Its precise force in either occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word’s ordinary meaning remains a literal fire.

d: Fleshly, carnal, earthly.

e.t: This word describes what is fleshly or material—something associated with ordinary human life and the physical realm. In the New Testament, it can describe bodily or worldly concerns, possessions, conduct, or resources, depending on the sentence. It occurs seven times in the Greek New Testament, so its central idea is consistent while its precise reference changes with context. The word does not by itself explain whether the matter is good or bad; the surrounding passage determines how this fleshly or material aspect is being discussed.

d: Full of darkness, dark.

e.t: This word means “dark,” describing something lacking light or brightness. It is an adjective, so it identifies a condition or quality rather than an action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Matthew 6:23 and Luke 11:34, 36. Its ordinary sense is straightforward: what is dark is not illuminated. The surrounding passage determines whether the word describes physical darkness or serves as an image for a person’s inner perception, but the central idea remains the absence of light.

d: A fellow elder.

e.t: This word means “fellow elder”: an elder who shares that role or standing with other elders. It identifies someone as belonging to the same group of elders, rather than merely referring to an elder in isolation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Peter 5:1. Its basic meaning emphasizes shared elder status; the precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: To dwell with, live in wedlock with.

e.t: This word means “to live with,” describing shared residence with another person. It refers to dwelling together rather than merely meeting or being near someone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its use in the sentence. The word appears in 1 Peter 3:7, but the available lexical meaning is best stated simply as living together with someone.

d: Welfare, prosperity, deliverance, preservation, salvation, safety.

e.t: Salvation means rescue or deliverance from danger, ruin, or the condition from which a person needs to be saved. In the Greek New Testament, it is a noun naming the saving result or state rather than the act of saving itself. The word is used 46 times in 45 verses, showing that salvation is a recurring New Testament subject. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains deliverance and the resulting well-being of those who are saved.

d: To tremble, to be afraid.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “to tremble,” describing someone who is physically shaking or quivering. It focuses on the visible act or condition of trembling rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, appearing in Mark, Luke, and 2 Peter. The surrounding verse determines what prompted the trembling in each occurrence, but the word itself centers on the bodily expression of shaking.

d: Show, display, pomp, imagination.

e.t: This word refers to pageantry or pomp—the impressive display, ceremony, and outward splendor associated with a public appearance. It describes more than simple presence: it draws attention through grandeur and display. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Acts 25:23, and the English rendering there is “pomp.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to a striking, formal, and showy presentation.

d: Haran.

e.t: Haran is a proper name, referring to the person or place identified by that name in the biblical account. It is rendered consistently as “Haran,” rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, the name occurs twice, both times in Acts 7:2 and Acts 7:4. Its exact significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function is simply to identify Haran by name.

d: Cold.

e.t: This word means cold, describing a condition of low temperature or the absence of warmth. It is used three times in the Greek New Testament, appearing once each in John, Acts, and 2 Corinthians. Its consistent rendering as cold supports this straightforward meaning. The surrounding verse determines whether it describes the weather, a physical setting, or a person’s experience of cold, but the word itself expresses coldness rather than warmth.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “originally”. It describes something happening at the beginning or “for the first time,” marking an earlier point in time or priority. As an adverb, it qualifies an action or statement by showing that it was true at the start, before later developments or circumstances. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 11:26, so its precise force there comes from the surrounding sentence. Its basic sense remains a straightforward reference to what happened first or was true originally.
